\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{hyperref}

\title{Neighbourhood Walkability and Incident Type~2 Diabetes:
A Five-Year Cohort Study in Three Municipal Districts}
\author{L.~Moreau, P.~Achterberg, and S.~Okafor}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We followed 8{,}412 adults free of diabetes at baseline across
three municipal districts for the period 2019-2023 to estimate
the association between neighbourhood walkability and incident
type~2 diabetes. Walkability was summarised with a composite
index of intersection density, land-use mix, and retail access.
During follow-up, 614 participants developed diabetes.
After adjustment for age, sex, income, and baseline body mass
index, residents of the most walkable tertile had a hazard ratio
of 0.82 (95\% CI 0.71--0.95) compared with the least walkable
tertile. Associations were stronger among participants aged
60 years and older. These findings support urban design as a
plausible lever for chronic disease prevention.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Type~2 diabetes accounts for a growing share of the
health care burden in mid-sized cities, and its incidence is
socially patterned along neighbourhood lines.
A growing literature links the built environment to metabolic
risk, but much of it is cross-sectional and therefore vulnerable
to reverse causation and residential self-selection.
Longitudinal designs with objective environmental measures
remain comparatively scarce, particularly outside North America.
The present study uses five years of follow-up from a
population-based cohort to examine whether residents of more
walkable neighbourhoods develop diabetes at lower rates,
and whether the association differs by age group.
We prespecified the age-stratified analysis because older
residents spend more of their daily time in the immediate
residential environment and may therefore be more sensitive
to features that facilitate or impede walking.

\section{data sources}
The cohort was assembled from the municipal health examination
programme, which invites all registered residents aged 45 to 74
to a baseline assessment every five years.
Of 14{,}036 invited residents, 9{,}880 attended the baseline
examination and 8{,}412 met the eligibility criteria for the
present analysis after excluding prevalent diabetes and those
with missing address histories.
Neighbourhood walkability was computed for each residential
address from the municipal geographic information system,
following the index construction of the national walkability
project, with intersection density measured within a 5 km
network buffer of each home.
Incident diabetes was ascertained from the linked outpatient
claims registry, which covers all residents regardless of the
sector in which their healthcare is delivered.

\section{Methods}
\subsection{Exposure and Outcome}
The walkability index was standardised within each district and
modelled both as a continuous score and as district-specific
tertiles.
Incident diabetes was defined as two outpatient claims with the
relevant diagnosis code at least ninety days apart,
or one filled prescription of glucose-lowering medication.
Follow-up time accrued from the baseline examination to the
first qualifying event, death, deregistration from the
municipality, or the administrative end of follow-up,
whichever came first.

\subsection{Statistical Analysis}
Cox proportional hazards models were fitted with district as a
stratification factor, allowing the baseline hazard to differ
across districts.
Models were adjusted for age, sex, household income quintile,
educational attainment, baseline body mass index, and smoking
status.
The proportional hazards assumption was assessed with
Schoenfeld residuals and was not violated for the exposure of
interest.
Effect modification by age was tested with a multiplicative
interaction term between walkability and the age indicator.

\section{Results}
\subsection{main findings}
During 39{,}580 person-years of follow-up, 614 incident cases of
diabetes were identified, corresponding to a crude incidence
rate of 15.5 per 1{,}000 person-years.
Screening uptake at baseline was close to 50 percent of the
invited population, with little variation across districts.
Participants in the most walkable tertile were more likely to
report walking for transport and lived, on average, within
5 km of a wider range of retail destinations than participants
in the least walkable tertile.
In the fully adjusted model, the hazard ratio for the highest
versus the lowest walkability tertile was 0.82 with a 95\%
confidence interval excluding the null.
The association was materially unchanged when the analysis was
restricted to participants who had not moved during follow-up,
which argues against strong residential self-selection.

\subsection{Age-Specific Estimates}
Among participants aged 60 years and older, the corresponding
hazard ratio was 0.74, whereas among younger participants it was
0.93 with a wider confidence interval.
The interaction term was statistically significant at the
conventional level.
A sensitivity analysis treating the index as a continuous score
yielded a consistent dose--response pattern across the observed
range of neighbourhood walkability.

\subsection{Placebo Comparison}
As a negative control, we repeated the analysis with incident
"placebo" outcomes---claims for acute injuries---for which no
association with walkability is expected, and found none.

\section{Discussion}
In this cohort, higher neighbourhood walkability was associated
with a modestly lower incidence of type~2 diabetes over five
years of follow-up, with the strongest associations among older
residents.
The magnitude of the association is comparable to that reported
in two recent North American cohorts, although our healthcare
context differs in ways that may attenuate or amplify the
underlying effect.
Several limitations temper causal interpretation: the  study
relied on claims-based outcome ascertainment, the walkability
index captures only some features of the pedestrian
environment, and residual confounding by diet and occupational
activity cannot be excluded.
Nonetheless, the negative-control analysis and the stability of
the estimates among non-movers lend the findings some
robustness, and the age pattern is biologically plausible given
the mobility constraints of older residents.

\section{Conclusion}
Walkable neighbourhood design was associated with a lower
incidence of type~2 diabetes in this municipal cohort,
particularly among older adults.
Urban planning that improves the pedestrian environment may
contribute to chronic disease prevention, and our healthcare
planning should take such environmental determinants into
account when allocating prevention resources.
\end{document}
